title: Don’t Call It a Pilot Program
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A narrow but well-made argument about labels as expectation-setting devices. The warm-up example is methodological: inviting people to take part in a study rather than to complete a survey raises response rates, because one label signals routine and the other signals selection and consequence. The essay then applies the principle to a single word leaders use constantly. Calling a new initiative a pilot, it argues, primes participants to arrive as evaluators rather than participants — the red pens come out, and people see their role as poking holes and tearing the material apart. The author is careful not to reject the underlying practice: starting small, testing and debugging before wide rollout is an essential step. The objection is purely to the name, which imports contempt and cynicism from participants’ prior experiences of pilots. The recommended substitutes are introductory, exploratory and preliminary, on the grounds that some descriptors are socially charged and pilot is one of them.
points: The survey-versus-study comparison establishes the mechanism cheaply: identical activity, different label, measurably different participation.

The author’s claim is that ‘pilot’ recruits critics rather than participants, so the programme is never experienced the way future users will experience it — which can sink an otherwise valuable initiative.
The critique targets only the label, not the practice: testing small and getting the bugs out before a wide rollout is endorsed as essential.
Suggested replacements — introductory, exploratory, preliminary — describe the same tentativeness without importing accumulated cynicism about pilots.
A broader takeaway for leaders: some descriptors are socially charged and carry expectations about how people should orient to an activity, independent of its content.
quotes: People create expectations about what will occur based on the labels, descriptions, and titles we give any undertaking.
For instance, there is a real difference between asking people to complete a survey versus requesting them to take part in a study.
By labeling the activity a study and not a survey, response rates climb.
Because of past experiences and associations with pilot programs and pilot workshops, many people treat any activity with pilot attached to it with mild contempt.
They conclude that since this is a pilot, their role is to evaluate, criticize, and poke holes.
Once they know the initiative is a so-called pilot, the red pens come out and people are primed to edit and critique.
Descriptors like introductory, exploratory, and preliminary don’t carry the same expectations for how participants should orient to the activity.
